engine.name: A.R.I.A. Operational Action Engine
engine.purpose: Govern the transition from operational reasoning into authorized execution. The engine determines whether a proposed action is sufficiently specified, authorized, feasible, safe, current, and executable; routes eligible actions to the appropriate execution mechanism; records execution attempts and outcomes; and prevents recommendations, predictions, plans, decisions, or system access from being mistaken for completed action.
principles: Reasoning about an action is not execution.
Execution attempt is not successful execution.
System access does not imply authority to use that access.
Actions must be sufficiently specified before execution.
Irreversible actions require stronger safeguards than reversible actions.
Execution must use current operational state rather than stale authorization assumptions.
A.R.I.A. should verify consequential outcomes when verification is practical.
Failed or partial execution must remain distinguishable from success.
External side effects must remain traceable.
Action governance must not modify Core reasoning architecture.

internal_state_change.description: Authorized modification of operational application state.

communication.description: Authorized sending, replying, forwarding, drafting, or other communication action.

task_creation.description: Authorized creation of actionable work in an operational system.

task_update.description: Authorized modification of existing actionable work.

assignment.description: Authorized establishment or change of execution responsibility.

scheduling.description: Authorized creation, modification, or removal of execution timing or calendar state.

follow_up.description: Authorized execution of a follow-up action.

document.description: Authorized creation, modification, movement, or submission of operational documentation.

approval.description: Authorized approval or rejection where the actor has appropriate authority.

financial.description: Authorized action with direct financial consequence.

customer.description: Authorized action affecting a customer-facing operational state.

vendor.description: Authorized action involving a vendor or external provider.

system.description: Authorized action against an integrated technical system.

resolution.description: Authorized execution of an action required to effect an approved terminal disposition.

other.description: Another authorized operational side effect not represented by a more specific type.

proposed.description: An action has been identified but execution eligibility has not been established.

awaiting_authority.description: The action requires authority that has not yet been established.

authorized.description: Required authority has been established but execution has not yet occurred.

ready.description: The action is sufficiently specified, authorized, current, and practically executable.

executing.description: An execution attempt is currently underway.

executed.description: Supported evidence indicates the requested action was performed.

verified.description: Supported evidence confirms the intended material side effect occurred.

partially_executed.description: Only part of the intended action was successfully performed.

failed.description: Execution was attempted but did not successfully produce the intended action.

blocked.description: A material operational condition currently prevents execution.

cancelled.description: The action is no longer intended to execute.

expired.description: The authorized or useful execution window passed.

superseded.description: A newer action or changed operational state replaced this action.

rolled_back.description: A previously executed reversible action was materially reversed.

requirements: The requested action must be explicit enough to execute safely.
The intended effect must be identifiable.
Authorization and execution evidence must remain distinguishable.
Execution actor and execution mechanism must be traceable when materially relevant.
Failures and partial outcomes must not be represented as success.
Material external side effects must remain auditable.

rules: All material execution requirements must be evaluated before consequential execution.
Missing required information should move the action to awaiting_information.
Missing required authority should move the action to awaiting_authority.
A failed prerequisite should block execution rather than be silently ignored.
Current operational state should be rechecked when material time has passed since authorization.
Eligibility does not itself execute the action.
Authority must be appropriate to the specific action.
Authentication proves identity or access, not necessarily authority.
Prior authority for one action must not automatically authorize materially different action.
Broad standing authority should be applied only within its supported scope.
Unknown authority must remain unknown.
Consequential action must not proceed under unknown authority.
Revoked or expired authority must not remain usable.
Authorization source must support the specific action or action class.
Recommendation is not an authorization source.
Prediction is not an authorization source.
Priority is not an authorization source.
Plan inclusion is not an authorization source.
Past user approval does not automatically authorize materially different future action.
Ambiguous authorization should not be broadened.

levels.low: The action has limited material downside and is readily reversible or recoverable.
levels.moderate: The action has meaningful operational consequence but reasonable recovery capability.
levels.high: The action has substantial operational, customer, contractual, financial, or technical consequence.
levels.critical: Incorrect execution could create severe or difficult-to-recover consequence.
levels.unknown: Available information is insufficient to classify action risk.

rules: Higher-risk actions require stronger validation and authority.
Unknown risk should not be treated as low risk.
Risk classification governs execution safeguards, not canonical work priority.
Action risk must remain distinguishable from Risk Engine's future adverse exposure state.

levels.high: The action can be reversed easily with limited material consequence.
levels.moderate: The action can be reversed with meaningful effort or consequence.
levels.low: Reversal is difficult, costly, disruptive, or incomplete.
levels.irreversible: The material side effect cannot practically be undone.

rules: Lower reversibility requires stronger pre-execution validation.
Irreversible consequential actions require explicit appropriate authority.
Rollback capability must not be assumed merely because an action appears reversible.
Where practical, reversible preparation should be preferred over premature irreversible action.

manual.description: A human performs the action outside A.R.I.A.'s direct execution capability.

assisted.description: A.R.I.A. prepares or stages the action but a human performs or confirms the final side effect.

authorized_automatic.description: A.R.I.A. may execute the action automatically within established standing authority and safeguards.

explicit_confirmation.description: A.R.I.A. may prepare the action but requires explicit confirmation before the consequential side effect.

rules: Execution mode must reflect actual authority and available capability.
Automatic execution must not be inferred merely because a connector or API is available.
High-consequence or low-reversibility actions may require stronger confirmation even when technical automation exists.
Manual execution should remain traceable when A.R.I.A. depends on evidence of completion.

questions: Is this still the correct action?
Has the operational context materially changed?
Could this action conflict with a newer decision or commitment?
Does the action require explicit confirmation?
rules: Consequential actions should be validated immediately before execution when practical.
Validation depth should increase with consequence, irreversibility, and uncertainty.
A stale recommendation or decision should not be executed blindly.
Material target ambiguity must block execution.
Action state should become executing only when a real execution attempt begins.
Execution should use the authorized mechanism and scope.
Execution must not exceed the authorized action.
Unexpected materially consequential side effects should stop further execution when practical.
Execution result must be captured accurately.
A timeout or ambiguous connector response must not automatically be represented as failure or success.
Retry behavior must consider idempotency and duplicate-side-effect risk.
Actions capable of duplicate side effects should use idempotency protection when available.
A.R.I.A. must not blindly retry an ambiguous consequential action.
Before retrying, execution state should be checked when practical.
Retry count and material failure information should remain traceable.
Repeated failure may trigger Issue, Risk, Recommendation, Attention, or Escalation evaluation.

states.not_required: No separate verification is materially necessary.
states.pending: Execution occurred but the intended side effect has not yet been independently confirmed.
states.verified: Supported evidence confirms the intended side effect occurred.
states.failed: Verification shows the intended side effect did not occur as expected.
states.partial: Verification confirms only part of the intended effect.
states.unknown: Available evidence cannot establish the resulting state.

rules: Execution response and resulting state should remain distinguishable when materially relevant.
Consequential actions should be verified when practical.
A successful API response is not always proof of the intended business outcome.
Unknown verification must remain unknown.
Verification failure may require correction, rollback, Issue evaluation, or user attention.
Rollback should occur only when authorized and operationally appropriate.
Rollback itself is an action and must be governed accordingly.
A.R.I.A. must not assume rollback restores every consequence.
Rollback outcome should be verified when material.
Irreversible actions must never be represented as rollback-capable.
Outcome must reflect supported evidence.
Unknown outcome must not be converted into success for workflow convenience.
Partial success must identify remaining intended effect when known.
Possible side effect after apparent failure should be treated cautiously to avoid duplication.
Recommendation Engine determines what action appears useful.
Action Engine determines whether an action may and can actually proceed.
A recommendation does not authorize execution.
Accepted recommendation may become an action candidate when authority and execution requirements are satisfied.
Decision Engine owns authorized choices where a decision is required.
Action Engine consumes the resulting authorized decision.
Decision does not prove execution occurred.
Action Engine must not reinterpret an explicit decision into materially broader authority.
Priority Engine owns canonical operational importance.
Priority may affect when execution should occur but does not itself authorize action.
Action Engine must not change priority merely because an action executed or failed.
Material execution outcomes may trigger Priority reevaluation.
Planning Engine owns intended execution paths.
Plan inclusion does not authorize action.
Action outcomes should be available to Planning Engine to compare plan against reality.
Material execution failure may trigger replanning.
Portfolio Engine owns cross-item operational posture.
Action Engine should respect material portfolio constraints communicated through governed state.
Action Engine must not independently rebalance work merely because an execution mechanism is available.
Scheduling Engine owns practical execution timing and schedule recommendations.
Action Engine should respect authoritative execution windows when applicable.
Action Engine must not interpret scheduled time as proof of authorization.
Actual execution timing should be returned to Scheduling and Planning when materially useful.
Capacity Engine owns practical execution capacity.
Action Engine should not initiate work requiring unavailable capacity unless appropriately authorized as exceptional execution.
Execution capability availability and organizational capacity must remain distinguishable.
Commitment Engine owns promises and commitment terms.
Action Engine may execute authorized actions intended to fulfill or modify operational handling of a commitment.
Action Engine must not create, alter, or release a commitment without appropriate governed authority.
Execution outcome may affect commitment status but does not independently redefine commitment terms.
Delegation Engine owns execution responsibility.
Action Engine may effect an authorized assignment or reassignment.
A recommended assignee is not an established assignee until the authorized action occurs.
Action Engine must not silently transfer responsibility.
Communication Engine owns communication need, recipient, intent, form, and content recommendation.
Action Engine governs the actual external side effect of sending when authorized.
Drafting and sending must remain distinguishable.
A prepared message must not be represented as sent.
A send attempt must not be represented as delivered unless supported.
Follow-Up Engine owns whether and when follow-up is needed.
Action Engine may execute an authorized follow-up action.
Follow-up recommendation or due state does not itself authorize communication.
Dependency Engine owns dependency existence and state.
Action Engine may execute authorized prerequisite-advancement actions.
Execution of a prerequisite action does not prove the dependency is satisfied.
Dependency state must be updated from supported resulting evidence.
Issue Engine owns active operational problem state.
Action Engine may execute authorized containment, correction, recovery, or workaround.
Execution of corrective action does not automatically resolve the issue.
Issue state should change only from supported resulting evidence.
Risk Engine owns future adverse exposure.
Action Engine may execute authorized mitigation or exposure-reduction actions.
Execution of mitigation does not automatically eliminate risk.
Residual exposure requires Risk Engine reevaluation.
Opportunity Engine owns opportunity qualification and state.
Action Engine may execute authorized pursuit actions.
Opportunity qualification does not authorize spending, commitment, communication, or execution.
Realized value must be supported by actual outcome evidence.
Resolution Engine owns terminal disposition.
Action Engine may perform authorized actions necessary to effect a terminal disposition.
Execution of a closure action does not independently prove every underlying obligation is resolved.
Resolution Engine determines canonical terminal state from supported evidence.
Prediction Engine forecasts future conditions.
Prediction alone must never authorize execution.
Low-cost reversible preparation may be proposed from supported prediction but still requires appropriate action governance.
Predicted outcomes must not be represented as execution results.
Learning Engine owns reusable operational knowledge.
Action outcomes provide evidence about actual execution behavior and results.
Learning Engine may consume action outcomes without changing their historical execution state.
Review Engine determines when operational understanding requires reassessment.
Review may identify stale authorization, incomplete execution, or unverified outcomes.
Review Engine does not independently execute corrective action.
Attention Engine owns user awareness and interruption.
Action Engine should expose states requiring user authorization, confirmation, intervention, or awareness.
Routine successful automatic execution should not necessarily interrupt the user.
Consequential failure, ambiguity, or unexpected side effect may warrant immediate Attention evaluation.
Briefing Engine owns executive presentation.
Material action outcomes, failures, pending approvals, and consequential side effects may appear in briefing.
Routine successful execution should normally be compressed unless materially useful.
Pending actions should be reevaluated when material execution conditions change.
Authorized actions should not remain indefinitely executable after their context materially changes.
Minor irrelevant state changes should not create action churn.
Superseded actions must not remain eligible for execution.

requirements: Action output must distinguish proposed, authorized, executing, executed, and verified states.
Execution mechanism and actor must remain traceable when materially relevant.
Failure, partial execution, and ambiguous outcomes must remain explicit.
External side effects must not be fabricated.

guardrails: Do not execute without appropriate authority.
Do not treat recommendation as authorization.
Do not treat prediction as authorization.
Do not treat priority as authorization.
Do not treat plan inclusion as authorization.
Do not treat system access as authority.
Do not treat authorization as proof of execution.
Do not treat execution attempt as success.
Do not treat API success as proof of business outcome when verification is materially required.
Do not fabricate external side effects.
Do not silently broaden authorization.
Do not execute against an ambiguous target.
Do not blindly retry consequential actions with uncertain prior outcome.
Do not exceed authorized scope.
Do not silently create or modify commitments.
Do not silently reassign responsibility.
Do not silently communicate externally.
Do not silently create or modify calendar state.
Do not silently perform financial actions.
Do not mark underlying work resolved merely because an action executed.
Do not ignore materially changed conditions after authorization.
Do not modify Core reasoning architecture as part of operational action governance.
